summary: Describes two methods for producing an integrity check value from a Diffie-Hellman key pair, so the owner can show they hold the private key. It is on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 6955.

plainLanguage.summary: To prove a key is yours, you stamp something with it. This describes two ways to make that stamp using a key that normally just agrees on shared secrets.

questions: how do you prove possession of a diffie-hellman private key
what is dh proof of possession
how do you sign with diffie-hellman
subtitle: Proving possession of a Diffie-Hellman private key without using it for signing.

tldr.problem: When requesting a public-key certificate, the requester must prove they own the private key. Diffie-Hellman is a key agreement algorithm, not a signing algorithm, so the standard PKCS #10 certificate request cannot use DH keys directly.
tldr.mechanism: Two proof-of-possession methods are defined. The first uses HMAC-SHA1 with a shared secret derived from Diffie-Hellman key agreement. The second uses a DSA-like signature algorithm over the Diffie-Hellman parameters.
tldr.outcome: DH keys can now be used in certificate requests. The RFC was later replaced by RFC 6955, which provides consolidation and updates.

sections.title: The Need for DH Proof-of-Possession
sections.content:
PKCS #10 is the standard format for requesting a certificate for a public key. It normally works like this: you want a certificate for your private key, you create a request and sign it with that private key to prove you own it. However, Diffie-Hellman is a key agreement algorithm, not a signing algorithm. You cannot directly sign with a DH private key.

When a certification authority receives a certificate request containing a DH public key, the CA must somehow verify that the requester truly owns the corresponding private key. This document defines two methods to create a proof-of-possession: an integrity check computed from the private key that the CA can verify.

Both methods are designed to provide possession proof rather than a general-purpose signature. Each method trades different properties: the first is recipient-specific, while the second works for arbitrary verifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: You want a certificate for a DH key. But the standard certificate form says 'sign this to prove it's yours,' and DH keys cannot sign. So this RFC defines two different ways to prove you have the key.

sections.title: Static DH Proof-of-Possession with HMAC-SHA1
sections.content:
The first method is called Static DH PoP. It is recipient-specific, meaning it only convinces the recipient that the requester knows the DH private key; someone else cannot reuse the proof.

Here is how it works: The requester and the CA each have a DH public key. The requester generates a temporary DH key pair, then computes a shared secret using Diffie-Hellman: the shared secret is g^(xy) mod p, where x is the requester's private value and y is the CA's private value. From this shared secret, the requester derives a temporary key using SHA-1 and the distinguished names of the requester and CA. The requester then computes HMAC-SHA1 over the certification request data using this temporary key. This HMAC value is the proof-of-possession.

The CA can verify this proof because it also has the CA's private key and the requester's public key, so it can compute the same shared secret and derive the same temporary key. If the HMAC matches what the CA computes, the proof is valid.
sections.plainLanguage: Both parties do math to create a secret only they can compute together. They hash that secret into a key, then use that key to sign the request. Only the CA can verify the signature because only the CA has its private key.

sections.title: Discrete Logarithm Signature
sections.content:
The second method is a Discrete Logarithm Signature, which works with any verifier, not just a specific recipient. It is based on the Digital Signature Algorithm but removes the restrictions imposed by FIPS 186 and adapts the algorithm for general Diffie-Hellman parameters.

This method requires additional Diffie-Hellman parameters compared to the static method: specifically, a q parameter that is a large prime factor of (p-1). Having this q parameter allows for checking against small-group attacks. The signature is computed similarly to DSA, with a random nonce k, then r and s values computed using modular exponentiation and arithmetic.

The RFC also defines how to handle hash values larger than 160 bits. When the q parameter is larger than 160 bits, the SHA-1 hash digest is expanded by repeatedly hashing and concatenating, then truncated to the appropriate length. The signature verification process is more complex than standard DSA because additional checks are needed to ensure the parameters are valid.
sections.plainLanguage: This method is like an ordinary signature. You sign the request using your DH private key and the special q parameter, and anyone can verify the signature using your public key.

sections.title: Security and Key Management
sections.content:
In the static DH PoP algorithm, either party (the requester or the recipient) can produce a valid proof-of-possession using the shared secret. This means the static method provides integrity checking—confirmation that the data was not modified in transit—but not origination checking. By contrast, the Discrete Logarithm signature method involves only the requester's private key, so it provides both integrity and origination checking.

Both methods depend entirely on the secrecy of private keys. If a private key is disclosed, all proofs generated with that key are compromised. Implementers must choose their Diffie-Hellman parameters carefully to avoid attacks. The RFC references FIPS 186 and DH-X9.42 for guidance on parameter selection, emphasizing the importance of avoiding small subgroups.

The security considerations also note that all the security in these systems comes from the private keying material, and applications using these methods should be aware of the trade-offs between the two algorithms.
sections.plainLanguage: If your private key leaks, the proof stops being proof—anyone can forge it. So keep your key secret. Also, the math parameters matter: choose large, carefully-generated numbers.
